title: The earth is family
hookLine: Arjuna asks who counts as his own, and an Upanishad answers wide
carry: vasudhaiva kutumbakam: the earth itself is family
tomorrow: Duryodhana's first move: does he speak, or look?
last: WANTING TO FIGHT, OR TO KNOW?

cards: At a wedding or a funeral, a seating chart quietly decides who counts as close family, and sometimes someone ends up hurt by where they're sitting. Arjuna draws his own chart on a battlefield.

Later in chapter one, he stops talking about armies and reaches for a different word: svajana, my own people. How could we be happy, he asks, having killed our own people? So: who counts as one's own?

teach.b: The line: svajanam hi katham hatva sukhinah syama madhava. Sva, own. Jana, people.
Svajana: one's own people, kin. Katham, how. Sukhinah syama, could we be happy.
Arjuna's circle is real, and the Gita lets his grief speak in full before anyone answers it. But Sanskrit also has a line that draws the circle wider.
It's in the Maha Upanishad: ayam nijah paro veti ganana laghuchetasam, udaracharitanam tu vasudhaiva kutumbakam. This one is mine, that one is a stranger: so the narrow-hearted count.
For those whose ways are generous, the earth itself is family. Vasudha, the earth. Kutumbakam, a family, a household.

Notice the word ganana, counting. The narrow heart in the line isn't wicked; it just counts small, and the generous one counts the whole earth. Now a neighbor tradition, saying something close in its own words.

In the Bible's book of Acts, Paul tells a crowd in Athens that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Both lines refuse to stop the family at the door.

teach.h: ONE MAKER, OR A WIDE HEART.
teach.b: Paul's line starts from where people come from: one Maker, one blood. The Upanishad's starts from how a person counts: the width of a heart. Neither one makes Arjuna's question go away.

teach.h: NOT STOPPING THE FAMILY AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: He still has to face it, on a battlefield, with family on both sides.

how: Some Hindus quote vasudhaiva kutumbakam at gatherings and in welcomes; readers of the Gita in order hear Arjuna's svajana question in full before chapter two begins the reply.

s: vasudhaiva kutumbakam comes from the Bhagavad Gita
it's from the Maha Upanishad, a different Sanskrit text.
Acts 17:26 says God made all nations of one blood
Paul's words in Athens, in the King James Bible.
the two lines say exactly the same thing

games.q: a cousin's wedding list is too long, and someone says 'cut anyone who isn't real family.' a relative quotes vasudhaiva kutumbakam. what's the fair reading of the line?
o: every guest list must include the whole town.
it's about how wide the heart counts, not a rule for seating.
it only applies to monks, not to families.
games.why: the verse sets the narrow count, mine and stranger, beside the generous one, the earth as family: a way of seeing, not a seating rule.

practice: Close your eyes, if that's comfortable. On each in-breath, bring to mind someone inside your own circle; on each out-breath, someone just outside it, a neighbor, a stranger from this week.
If eyes open is easier, rest them on the floor in front of you. Let the circle widen a little with each breath, without forcing it.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Gita's first chapter: today, svajana, one's own people, and a wider line from another Sanskrit text, vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the earth is family.

orig.note: Sanskrit: svajana, one's own people, from sva, own, and jana, people; Arjuna's word in chapter one.

carryVoice: Pocket this: vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the earth itself is family. The circle can be wider than the chart.
